Time to the first audio chunk, not whole-call latency. Only scenarios that set a first-audio ceiling are streamed, so only those appear here.

Two stopwatches, two different questions

Every clip on this page was timed. The scenarios where a quick reply matters were timed twice, because "how fast is the model" is two questions, and they have very different answers.

Whole call asks: how long until the finished audio file is back? Like downloading a song before you can press play. This is the Latency row in the metric table, and every clip in the study has it.
First audio asks: how long until the listener hears the first word? Like a phone call: the person on the line hears you start speaking; they do not wait for you to finish. This is the panel above, and it exists for the scenarios that need a quick reply.

On this page: elevenlabs-v4 says its first word after a median 1169 ms and hands back the finished clip after 3.5 s; gemini-3-8-flash-tts says its first word after a median 1294 ms and hands back the finished clip after 3.7 s. The two models are 125 ms apart at the first word and 0.3 s apart at the finished file, and the same model is ahead on both. No streamed clip on either model reached the first word inside its scenario's ceiling.

How we measured it

  1. Same script, same voice, same model. For the 209 scenarios that need a quick reply, we asked each model to stream: send sound as soon as it has some, instead of the whole file at the end. Nothing else about the request changed.
  2. The clock starts when we send the request, before the connection is even open, so the network and the server's thinking time are all inside the number.
  3. The clock stops at the first piece of actual sound, not at a header or an empty message that arrives first.
  4. We keep listening until the clip ends, so the same clip also has a whole-call time. The two are stored side by side and never overwrite each other.
  5. Each of these scenarios sets a ceiling — 300 ms for the game line, 1000 ms for the conversational ones. A clip over its ceiling fails that gate like any other gate.
  6. Measured the same way on both models, from the same machine. This is the ordinary HTTP stream. It is not ElevenLabs' WebSocket real-time product, so the sub-second figures ElevenLabs publishes for that product are not what this panel measures.

Footnotes — what was assumed (223 scenarios · 459 clips · 203 runs).
Totals: generation $3.1854 · judging $0.5132 (kept separate; add them yourself if you must).
Models: gemini-3-8-flash-tts (Google; Gemini API · no region choice) · elevenlabs-v4 (ElevenLabs; ElevenLabs direct API · us).
Judge: gemini-2.5-flash (temperature 0) — same judge, same rubric, blind shuffled labels for every output.
The judge is uncalibrated. The 2-humans x 5-clips gate has never been run, so naturalness and clarity carry no evidence of agreement with a human ear.
Quality is meaned over scored cells only, and always carries its denominator. A gated cell is counted in the gate rate, never averaged into quality - a clean read that is too long for an ad slot is the wrong length, not bad audio.
A repeat is the same script and the same gates. Runs of an edited scenario are excluded from every spread on this page.
The objective audio number is a signal metric, not a MOS. It measures SNR, spectral flatness, clipping and bandwidth - it must not be quoted as a mean opinion score.
Cost is what the run believed it paid, at the rates frozen in its own manifest; cost per clip includes transcription and judging.
Judged by gemini-2.5-flash, listening to the audio, blinded A/B/C per scenario. It shares a vendor with one arm under test - blinding hides the label, not the acoustic fingerprint, so judge-derived criteria carry that exposure.
Transcribed by large-v3, run locally. The transcript is the basis of every WER number and every phrase gate.
Transcription cost on this page: $0.0000 (inside the cost per clip).
Effective per-scenario weights (incl. redistributed ones) are in manifest.json; every number traces to a JSONL row in the run folder. Outputs are immutable — a correction is a new run.
